My first job out of college was for a small division of a non-profit; without going into the details, our 15 or so employees made the great majority of the money that kept the entire 70-person organization afloat.

I had a great job, and a great boss; I was a cheap, trainable hire, and I stayed late for no extra money many nights while we launched a new product that succeeded beyond almost anyone’s wildest expectations.

After the launch, I often worked extra hours to make sure that the work was being done on time; I wanted to do my part to make sure that the product was well-received and work was done on time for our customers.
It was a heady time, with my first “real” paycheck, and a success that I helped in a small part to make a reality.
I had (and still do have) one bad habit: I’d show up at 7:58 am, 8:03 am, 8:11 am, 8:20 am, 8:02 am, etc.—I was supposed to be there by 8:00.

Others in other departments complained, many because they were resentful of the wages that people in our department were being paid (my salary doubled in my first nine months, and I was still “underpaid” by industry standards).
My boss shut down any and all complaints by responding that I was one of his best employees, and if I needed a little leeway, he was happy to give it.
No, he didn’t have to, and I wasn’t about to leave, but I suppose he saw some value in the extra hours that I worked, sometimes requested, sometimes not.
Then our division was sold.
It seems we were making too much money and the non-profit status of the entire organization was in jeopardy.
So we (our division and product) were sold to a small company in Ohio, and my dream job in Colorado changed to a more ho-hum affair in Ohio.
Never mind, it was still a great gig, and I was one of the fortunate ones chosen to make the move, and my move was paid for.
My boss and friend, a lifelong Colorado resident, made the move to Ohio, but his family didn’t.
As expected, eleven months later he quit and moved back to Colorado, after doing his best to situate us with the new company and its designs for our services.
A new boss from the new company was appointed.
He was a nice enough guy, trying to make a go in late middle age with a cheap company run by a somewhat greedy family (the kids and their spouses were in charge by then; the founders had retired).
Our wages were cut (we were reminded that we were always free to leave if we wanted to; this was the 1991 recession, after all).
It was still a good job, but the breaking point (for me) came when my (new) boss started to hassle me about when I arrived at work.
He was “old-school,” and never mind that I often stayed until 6:30 pm or later to get the work done (with a 4:30 pm quitting time); he was enraged every time I showed up at 8:03 am or 8:07 am.

We now had magnetic cards that granted us access each time we employees entered and left the premises, and instead of trying to figure out how he could fix our grenading revenues caused by the transfer of ownership and loss of confidence in our product, he was busy with computer printouts, trying to figure out how to make sure everyone was at their desk by 8 am, and complying with endless analysis requests from the family that owned us and a number of other smallish enterprises.
This new company liked meetings a lot.
I was called into his office, and he threatened my job over this issue.

He definitely had the right to do that, and I made sure from then on that I arrived at around 7:45, and sat in my car with the engine idling and the heat on until 7:59 am, at which point I got out of the car, swiped my card, and went to work.
I also made sure I left by 4:30 each day.
No more extra free time from me.
And I began to explore other options.
One night as I was leaving, this boss came running down the stairs as I was heading out the door at 4:32, begging me to stay.

All his star on-time arrivals had been out the door at 4:30 sharp, and due to insurance requirements for the work that we did, at least two people had to be in the building at all times, or the alarm had to be set, with everyone gone.
There were no exceptions.
He had to finish something up and wondered if I could hang out for a half-hour.

I pointed at my watch, said “It’s 4:30, but I’ll be happy to help you out with it at 8 am tomorrow,” and marched out the door, with our insurance not in effect until he could wrap things up and leave.
I was called into his office the next morning, and I figured I was going to lose my job.
I didn’t care; I was mentally ready to quit, and had been saving hard ever since the change in ownership.
I was ready to survive an extended period of unemployment.
But, I’d won the battle.
He was willing to go back to the “way things were” when he got a good 8–12 “free” hours out of me every week.
That was fine with me, and I stayed around for another couple of years, but my desire to put the company first was long gone.
I did my work, they loved it, and offered me a raise to somewhere above where I’d been prior to the pay cut I’d been given two years before on the day that I handed in my letter of resignation.
I at age 25 was the second of the “old guard” to leave , and the company, which still exists, has floundered through two more changes in ownership in the ensuing years.

It has never matched the level of success that we had at the “beginning,” although its now-previous owner (who bought it from the company that I worked for in Ohio) did lay off quite a few employees on December 26 a few years back.
I didn’t quit because I was underpaid (which I was).
I didn’t quit because they insisted I arrive on the dot at 8 am (I would have complied).

I quit because every move I made was, with the change in ownership, watched, and everything I did, on “their” time or on “my” time, was expected to be for the benefit of the company, and the “extra” hours that I once worked willingly were now expected…the polite “will you”’s of my first boss had been replaced with much more insistent “you will”’s from the new organization.
Maybe other people think differently, but I work to live; I don’t live to work.
Even working for myself, I insist on time away from my work, when I am accountable to no one.

I’m not some ultra-successful entrepreneur who has created some wildly successful business, but I have managed to create a job for myself, with better wages by far, that has lasted now for over 25 years, and I’ve not once had to explain why my commitment to work is over when I decide to leave.
I’ve had plenty of job offers (and accepted none), and I’ve even done some contract work, but it’s always been on my terms since May 1993.
I’ve taken a lot of time off, and will retire very early, compared to most people.
People need balance in their lives.
This means time away from work.
Or, conversely, for many retired people, it may mean some structure than includes work, whether it’s a job or a volunteer opportunity.
Some people are better at it than others.
It sounds like your two employees are pretty bright, and good at it.
All work + no play = burnout, at least for most people.
If you insist that these two employees’ commitment to work last beyond work hours on a regular basis, prepare to lose them, and also prepare to likely attract mediocre, but compliant employees.
This did absolutely nothing to promote productivity.
The slackers figured out pretty damn quickly that to stay in the CEO’s good graces, all they really had to do was be at their desk and look like they were working.
For the rest of us, we worked our asses off to pick up the slack and got no recognition.
The burnout rate at this place was astronomical.
Quit using desk-time as measure of productivity and switch to a results-oriented mindset.

At first I thought this question was a joke.
You have good employees they are doing the job and not sneaking off early or coming in late.
And yet you want to complain about it?

Look 30+ years ago when I started, one of my first bosses said “as salaried people we need to set an example even the lowest of us .. so if you aren’t working at least 45–50 hours each week you aren’t committed to the job”.
And they pushed people to squeeze those extra hours out, that extra commitment, the whole the job comes first attitude.
But this is a new era.
Companies have all backed off on that junk.
They recognize people who work like that are often more stressed, less healthy, and make more mistakes.
It’s NOT worth the extra hours as it often leads to worse outcomes down the line.
Welcome to the world of Life Balance (it’s not even work-life balance anymore .. it’s Life Balance).
And Covid and remote work have pushed this even more!
People do not want to waste time coming into and office when they can work from home.
They have higher morale and are more productive in many cases working from home.
Oh there are bastions of the old “work til you drop” attitude.
Goldman Sachs for example expects those people wanting to advance up their career ladder in their company to work 80+ hours a week.
And they want people in the office to install that mind control .. sorry culture .. on the employees.
But even they are starting to see people say nope, the money you offer is not worth it to my health and my life.
Those with visions of King Midas in their mind still do it.
But you can’t trust people so focused on money as it does cloud their vision and ethics.
So you go ahead, take two good employees, and try to pressure them to do more.
Just get ready to start shopping for new ones once they leave to go work for someone who cares about their employees.
